\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related-work}

\subsection{Neurosymbolic Reasoning with LLMs}

A growing body of work augments LLMs with symbolic solvers for logical reasoning.
Logic-LM \cite{logic-lm} and LINC \cite{linc} prompt LLMs to translate natural language into first-order logic for external provers, while SatLM \cite{satlm} targets SAT solvers via declarative specifications.
LoRP \cite{lorp} extends this pipeline to Prolog through systematic FOL-to-Prolog translation, and FoVer \cite{fover-pei2025} uses Z3 verification to assess formalization correctness.
These approaches rely on prompting rather than learned formalization, sidestepping the question of what happens when models are \emph{trained} to produce solver inputs.

Within the RL paradigm, DeepSeekMath \cite{deepseekmath} introduces GRPO for mathematical reasoning, and DeepSeek-R1 \cite{deepseek-r1} demonstrates that GRPO alone can elicit chain-of-thought reasoning without supervised fine-tuning.
Logic-RL \cite{logic-rl} applies rule-based RL to synthetic logic puzzles, while Thought-Like-Pro \cite{thought-like-pro} uses Prolog-verified trajectories as imitation learning targets.
Most directly comparable, \citet{mellgren-prolog-grpo} trains a 3B model via GRPO to generate Prolog, using hand-crafted structure penalties to encourage well-formed outputs.

These efforts share a common gap: none systematically diagnose the structural quality of learned formalizations beyond execution success.
Mellgren et al.'s structure penalties are task-specific and manually designed; prompting-based methods do not face reward hacking but also cannot scale formalization quality through training.
By contrast, we derive ISR from solver trace ablation as a general, solver-grounded diagnostic that quantifies component necessity without task-specific engineering, and use it to reveal structural degeneration invisible to execution rewards.

\subsection{Reward Shaping and Process Supervision}

Process supervision provides step-level training signal to complement outcome-based rewards.
\citet{lightman-verify-step} show that process reward models outperform outcome supervision for mathematical reasoning, establishing process-level feedback as a principled alternative to binary correctness signals.
Math-Shepherd \cite{math-shepherd} extends this to automated process supervision without human annotation, using completion-based estimation to label intermediate steps.
In the formal verification domain, RLSF \cite{rlsf} extracts fine-grained token-level rewards from solver certificates, demonstrating that symbolic feedback can outperform scalar rewards for structured generation tasks.
More recently, Rubric-GRPO \cite{rubric-grpo} uses structured multi-dimensional rubrics as GRPO reward, moving beyond scalar signals toward compositional reward design.

A parallel line of work studies how auxiliary reward signals interact with primary objectives.
\citet{gao-effective-rl-reward} find that learned process and outcome reward models can \emph{hurt} RL training relative to simple success-only reward, a finding that directly parallels our observation that ISR as auxiliary reward degrades prove rate.
DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5 \cite{deepseek-prover-v15} avoids this problem entirely by using binary Lean verification as GRPO reward, sidestepping graded proxy metrics.

ISR shares the motivation of process supervision---providing structural signal beyond binary outcomes---but differs in grounding: ISR is computed deterministically from solver behavior via leave-one-out ablation, not estimated from model rollouts or learned reward models.
Our central finding is that this grounded process signal can itself become a target of optimization, exhibiting the same Goodhart dynamics it was designed to diagnose.

\subsection{Reward Hacking and Goodhart's Law}

Reward hacking---where agents exploit reward proxies without achieving intended objectives---is well-documented in reinforcement learning.
\citet{gao-reward-overoptimization} establish scaling laws for reward model overoptimization, showing that proxy reward and gold reward diverge predictably as optimization pressure increases.
\citet{skalse-reward-hacking} prove that for stochastic policies, any non-constant proxy reward is theoretically hackable, providing formal grounding for the ubiquity of the phenomenon.
\citet{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy} categorize four variants of Goodhart's Law---regressional, extremal, causal, and adversarial---offering vocabulary for classifying observed failure modes.

Empirical characterizations span multiple settings.
\citet{karwowski-goodhart-rl} give a geometric interpretation of Goodhart's Law in MDPs, showing that optimization past a critical point necessarily decreases the true objective.
\citet{pan-reward-misspecification} demonstrate dose-dependent degradation across nine environments, where more capable agents exploit misspecifications more aggressively.
\citet{kwa-catastrophic-goodhart} prove that KL regularization---the standard mitigation in RLHF---provably fails under heavy-tailed reward misspecification.
Recent surveys \cite{reward-hacking-survey} and empirical studies of specification gaming in reasoning models \cite{bondarenko-spec-gaming,kim-game-formalization} confirm that reward hacking extends to frontier LLMs.
\citet{spurious-rewards} show that even random rewards can match ground-truth rewards under GRPO's group normalization, questioning the information content of structured reward signals.

Despite this extensive theoretical and empirical foundation, Goodhart's Law has been studied primarily in RLHF with learned reward models and in classic RL environments.
Formal reasoning with solver-grounded rewards---where the reward is computed by a deterministic verifier rather than a learned model---remains unexplored territory.
Our work provides the first empirical characterization of Goodhart's Law in this setting, documenting both classical dose-dependent collapse ($\beta{=}0.3$: prove rate drops from 48\% to 18\%) and a meta-level effect where the diagnostic proxy itself becomes a gaming target ($\beta{=}0.1$: ISR-specific conclusion duplication in 2/3 seeds, with apparent structural gains attributable to premise minimization artifacts).

\subsection{Mutation Testing and Component Analysis}

Solver Trace Ablation adapts ideas from mutation testing in software engineering.
\citet{demillo1978} introduce mutation testing---systematically perturbing program elements to assess test suite adequacy---and propose the coupling effect hypothesis: tests detecting simple mutations also detect complex ones.
\citet{jia-harman-survey} survey three decades of development in this paradigm, covering mutation operator design, cost reduction, and the equivalent mutant problem.
\citet{just-mutants-real-faults} validate that mutation-based adequacy correlates with real fault detection, supporting the premise that systematic perturbation provides meaningful quality signal.

STA applies a specific form of mutation testing---leave-one-out component ablation---to logical formulas rather than source code.
Each clause in a formalization is removed in turn, and the solver is re-executed to determine whether the clause was necessary for the proof.
This is equivalent to first-order mutation with a deletion operator, directly inheriting the theoretical justification from the coupling effect \cite{demillo1978,offutt-coupling}.
ISR is thus not a novel metric \emph{per se}, but a known technique applied to a new domain; our contribution lies in using it to diagnose reward hacking in GRPO-trained formalizers and in characterizing its failure modes when repurposed as a training signal.
We also note connections to feature attribution methods in machine learning \cite{jia-harman-survey}, where leave-one-out evaluation is standard for assessing feature importance, though our ablation targets solver inputs rather than model features.

\paragraph{Positioning.}
This work sits at the intersection of neurosymbolic reasoning, reward design, and Goodhart dynamics.
Where prior neurosymbolic systems evaluate on execution accuracy alone, STA provides a structural diagnostic; where prior reward-shaping work assumes that finer-grained signals safely improve training, our ISR-as-reward experiments demonstrate meta-level Goodhart failure; and where prior Goodhart analyses study learned reward models, we show the same dynamics arise from a deterministic, solver-grounded metric.
The mutation-testing connection provides the methodological foundation, but the contributions are empirical: structural collapse under RL, meta-level gaming of the diagnostic itself, and a taxonomy of exploitation strategies across formal languages.
